At a glance

Best months
  • December to March and July to August for the driest weather
  • September to April for the northern migrants
Regions
Santa Marta and the Sierra NevadaLa Guajira and the Caribbean dry forestThe Perija MountainsThe Magdalena valley and the Chicamocha canyonThe Eastern Andes and BogotaThe Central Andes: Manizales and Rio BlancoThe Coffee Region: Otun Quimbaya and MontezumaThe Western Andes and JardinThe Cauca valley and the Km 18 cloud forestNarino and the southern Pacific slopeThe Choco and the Pacific coastThe Llanos: Meta and CasanareThe Amazon: Leticia and Amacayacu
Routes
A Bogota Layover1 dayThe Santa Marta Endemics5 daysThe Llanos6 daysLeticia and the Amazon6 daysThe Coffee Triangle Loop8 daysNorth and Centre14 daysThe Full Country21 days
Getting around
Bogota is the hub and domestic flights are cheap and frequent. The Andes are three separate ranges with deep valleys between them, so a road route between two of them takes a day.

When to Go

Colombia sits on the equator, so the year turns on rain rather than on temperature and every altitude keeps its own climate all year. The dry spells are December to March and July to August, and northern migrants are in the country from September to April.

The northern dry season

December to March

The Caribbean coast, La Guajira and the Andean valleys dry out, roads harden, and northern migrants are still in the country.

Go for The most reliable weather of the year, dry tracks into the Sierra Nevada and the Perija, and warblers alongside the residents.

Trade off Colombian and international holidays fill lodges around Christmas and Easter, so book the reserve beds early.

Typical daily average
  • Santa Marta: 19 to 28 °C / 66 to 82 °F
  • Bogota: 8 to 19 °C / 46 to 66 °F
  • Manizales: 13 to 22 °C / 55 to 72 °F

The Andean rains

April to June and September to November

Rain builds through the afternoons in the mountains while the mornings often stay clear, and the forest is at its loudest.

Go for Birds are nesting and singing, fruiting is heavy, and the hummingbird feeders are busy all day.

Trade off Afternoon downpours cut birding short, and unpaved mountain roads can close after a heavy night.

Typical daily average
  • Manizales: 13 to 22 °C / 55 to 72 °F
  • Bogota: 9 to 19 °C / 48 to 66 °F
  • Quibdo: 23 to 31 °C / 73 to 88 °F

The Pacific whale season

July to October

Humpbacks calve along the Choco coast, the Pacific lodges open their season, and southbound migration reaches the Andes.

Go for Whales from the same boats that reach the forest, and a strong passage of northern migrants from September.

Trade off The Choco is one of the wettest places on earth in any month, and flights there are small and weather dependent.

Typical daily average
  • Quibdo: 23 to 31 °C / 73 to 88 °F
  • Leticia: 22 to 31 °C / 72 to 88 °F
  • Santa Marta: 19 to 29 °C / 66 to 84 °F

Where to Bird

Colours match each region. Select a marker to open its entry below.

One pin per region, and the national parks and stops inside each region card carry their own coordinates. The three Andean cordilleras run north to south through the middle of the map, so a pair of regions that look close together can sit on opposite sides of a mountain range.

A Bogota Layover

Bogota (BOG), the eastern hills or the savanna wetlands, back to the terminal

Bogota sits at 2,600 metres with Andean forest half an hour above it. A morning on the La Calera road or at the city wetlands reaches high Andean birds and gets you back for an afternoon flight.

The Full Country

Santa Marta (SMR), the Sierra Nevada 3 nights, the Magdalena 2 nights, Bogota 3 nights, Manizales 3 nights, Jardin 2 nights, Cali 3 nights, the Choco 4 nights, Bogota (BOG) out

Three weeks and several internal flights. The route reaches all three Andean ranges, the Caribbean, the inter-Andean valleys and the Pacific, and the Choco leg depends on weather and small aircraft.

Santa Marta and the Sierra Nevada

Cloud forest and paramo edge above Minca, reached by 4x4 in under two hours from Santa Marta

An isolated massif that climbs from the Caribbean to snow in forty kilometres, cut off from the Andes for long enough to grow its own birds. More species live here and nowhere else than in any comparable piece of ground on earth.

  • Habitat: Mangrove-lined lagoons, freshwater marsh and arid woodland run along the coast and rise within a few kilometres into subtropical and temperate forest on slopes that reach 5,800 m. Sixteen of Colombia's fifty-nine endemics live on this one massif.
  • When: Good all year. Santa Marta Parakeet, White-tailed Starfrontlet and Santa Marta Antbird hold the ground through the year.
  • Getting there: One rough road climbs the north-west side and is not always open; four-wheel drive is advisable in the September to December wet season. Turn south off the Riohacha road a few kilometres east of Santa Marta towards Minca, bird the roadside forest over the 13 km to the village, then keep left at every fork after 26 km and work the road from km 32 to km 42.
  • Look for: Santa Marta Parakeet, White-tailed Starfrontlet, Santa Marta Antbird, Santa Marta Screech Owl, Santa Marta Sabrewing, Santa Marta Blossomcrown
  • National parks:
    • Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta National Natural Park, A national park with entry controlled through indigenous territory, visited only with an authorised guide. Cloud forest and paramo higher up hold the range's rarest endemics.
    • El Dorado Reserve (ProAves)
    • Tayrona National Natural Park, A national park with an entry fee and marked trails through dry forest to the coast. Dry forest specialities and mixed flocks work the trail edges near the beaches.
  • Stops:
    • : A coffee-growing town in the Sierra Nevada foothills, free to reach by road from Santa Marta and the usual base. Feeder trails and tanager flocks sit close to every guesthouse.
    • : A working historic coffee estate above Minca, walked freely along its own roads or with a farm guide. Mixed flocks and hummingbirds work the shade coffee.
    • : A ridge-top hamlet above Minca, by 4x4 or on foot, birded freely from the open track. Cloud forest tanagers and mixed foliage-gleaner flocks move through.
    • Cerro Kennedy, El Dorado Reserve : A ProAves reserve booked ahead and usually stayed in overnight. It is the most reliable place anywhere for Santa Marta Parakeet and White-tailed Starfrontlet.
    • : A coffee-farming village on the park's southern flank, on rough road and birded from tracks through farmland. Santa Marta Antbird and understorey flocks hold the forest edge.
    • Via Parque Isla de Salamanca : Mangrove and lagoon on the road between Barranquilla and Santa Marta. A boardwalk trail leads off the highway.
  • Visitor centres: El Dorado Reserve Ecolodge (ProAves)
  • Also covers: Cerro Kennedy, El Dorado Reserve, El Dorado Reserve (ProAves), El Dorado Reserve Ecolodge (ProAves), La Victoria coffee farm, Minca, Palmor, San Lorenzo ridge, Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta National Natural Park, Tayrona National Natural Park, Via Parque Isla de Salamanca
  • Also watch for: The forest still holds cougar, tapir and brocket deer, all rarely seen, alongside two harlequin toads found nowhere else on earth and most vocal in the wetter months around April to June and September to November. Howler monkeys and the mountain's own anole lizards are easier company on the lower trails around Minca.

La Guajira and the Caribbean dry forest

Desert scrub, dry forest and coastal lagoons across the Guajira Peninsula, a half day's drive from Santa Marta

Thorn scrub, salt flats and cactus on a flat peninsula reaching towards Venezuela. The birds here belong to the dry Caribbean rather than the Andes, and most of them can be watched from the roadside in an easy morning.

  • Habitat: Desert scrub runs east from Santa Marta along the Caribbean shore and holds a set of specialities shared only with northwest Venezuela. Marsh and woodland line the coastal road west towards Barranquilla.
  • When: Good all year. Vermilion Cardinal, Buffy Hummingbird and Tocuyo Sparrow stay through the year.
  • Getting there: Good patches of scrub sit at km 130 and km 140 from Santa Marta, about 20 km west of Riohacha, and the 95 km coast road west to Barranquilla runs alongside the marshes.
  • Look for: Vermilion Cardinal, Buffy Hummingbird, Tocuyo Sparrow, Chestnut Piculet, White-whiskered Spinetail, American Flamingo
  • National parks:
    • Los Flamencos Fauna and Flora Sanctuary, A national sanctuary with an entry fee and marked boardwalks through the lagoons. Vermilion Cardinal and Buffy Hummingbird work the surrounding dry scrub alongside the flamingos.
    • Macuira National Natural Park
  • Stops:
    • : A fishing village on the edge of Los Flamencos sanctuary, walked freely along the lagoon shore. American Flamingo holds the water with a full supporting cast of herons and shorebirds.
    • : The regional capital, with a seafront malecon and salt pans on its outskirts, all walked freely. Waders and terns work the shoreline among the fishing boats.
    • : The unofficial Wayuu capital and the last sizeable town before the open desert, free to reach by road. It is the stop for fuel and a guide before the track into Macuira.
    • : A salt-producing town on the desert coast, its evaporation pans walked freely from the road. Shorebird flocks and the odd flamingo work among the salt pyramids.
    • : A beach town where dry forest meets the coast, birded freely along farm tracks behind the village. Chestnut Piculet and White-whiskered Spinetail work the scrub.
  • Also covers: Camarones, Los Flamencos Fauna and Flora Sanctuary, Macuira National Natural Park, Manaure salt flats, Palomino, Riohacha, Uribia
  • Also watch for: American flamingos gather by the thousand in the lagoons of Los Flamencos, in the greatest numbers between November and March as birds move in from colonies in Venezuela. Green and hawksbill turtles nest on the desert beaches around the same months, and crab-eating foxes and Guajiran iguanas are common along the dry scrub tracks.

The Perija Mountains

Remote cloud forest and paramo on the Venezuelan border, reached by 4x4 from Valledupar

A range on the Venezuelan border with its own set of endemics, described and named only in the last two decades. Access is by rough track and needs arranging ahead, which is why so few people have birded it.

  • Habitat: The Serrania del Perija runs for some 300 km along the Venezuelan border at the northernmost extension of the Andes and reaches around 3,600 metres. The range is poorly researched and carries high floral and faunal endemism, along with wide mountain views.
  • When: Good all year. Perija Metaltail, Perija Thistletail and Perija Brushfinch are here in every month.
  • Getting there: Approach the range from Valledupar. Security kept the area closed until recently, so tourist infrastructure is thin and private reserves are only slowly emerging. Accommodation is humble and the lodges have to be reserved in advance because of the remoteness. Guides are usually available at the site.
  • Look for: Perija Metaltail, Perija Thistletail, Perija Brushfinch, Perija Tapaculo
  • National park: Chamicero de Perija Reserve (ProAves)
  • Stops:
    • : The regional capital and the usual starting point for a Perija trip, by air or road. It is the base for arranging the 4x4 and guide the mountains require.
    • : A foothill town on the road toward the range, passed through freely. Dry scrub and farmland typical of the Cesar valley floor run out here before the climb begins.
    • : A small town on the road up into the range, passed through freely. It is the last stretch of open farmland before the climate turns cool and cloud forest begins.
    • : The last town before the mountains proper, free to reach by road. It is the gateway where a 4x4 and local guide are arranged for the climb to the reserve.
    • Chamicero de Perija Reserve : A ProAves reserve booked ahead and usually stayed in overnight. Cloud forest and subparamo hold Perija Metaltail, Perija Thistletail and Perija Brushfinch.
    • : A village on the range's southern approach, birded from farm tracks by road with a local guide's permission. Foothill species hold it, wood-quail and screech-owls among them.
  • Visitor centres: Chamicero de Perija Reserve Lodge (ProAves)
  • Also covers: Agustin Codazzi, Chamicero de Perija Reserve (ProAves), Chamicero de Perija Reserve Lodge (ProAves), La Jagua de Ibirico, La Paz, La Victoria de San Isidro, Manaure Balcon del Cesar, Valledupar
  • Also watch for: The reserve forest at Chamicero de Perija still holds a population of brown spider monkeys, critically endangered and rarely seen elsewhere in Colombia, along with puma and a butterfly fauna that peaks in the wetter months from April to June. Glass frogs and harlequin frogs are easiest to find around the reserve's streams at dawn.

The Magdalena valley and the Chicamocha canyon

Dry canyon scrub and lowland Magdalena forest between Bucaramanga and the Rio Claro karst

The great river valley that splits the Eastern and Central Andes. It holds humid forest at Rio Claro and dry canyon scrub around Chicamocha, two habitats that share almost nothing, a few hours apart.

  • Habitat: The mid Magdalena valley holds the last remnants of lowland tropical rainforest in this part of Colombia. The Pauxi Pauxi reserve near Bucaramanga covers about 1,940 hectares of tropical rainforest and lower cloud forest between 200 and 1,500 metres. On the western side of the valley the Rio Claro reserve protects 500 hectares of ancient rainforest around a canyon cut by a clear river, and more than 540 bird species have been recorded there.
  • When: Good all year. Niceforo's Wren, Chestnut-bellied Hummingbird and Velvet-fronted Euphonia are on site in all twelve months.
  • Getting there: Rio Claro sits on the Bogota to Medellin highway, 263 km from Bogota and 152 km from Medellin, with accommodation in and around the reserve and guides for hire locally. The Pauxi Pauxi reserve has limited accommodation on site.
  • Look for: Niceforo's Wren, Chestnut-bellied Hummingbird, Velvet-fronted Euphonia, Colombian Chachalaca
  • National parks: Chicamocha Canyon (Parque Nacional del Chicamocha), Reserva Natural Canon del Rio Claro El Refugio, ProAves Cucarachero de Chicamocha Reserve
  • Stops:
    • : A dry forest plateau above the canyon rim, with farmland and scrub tracks walked freely from the road. Chestnut-bellied hummingbird and other dry canyon specialities work the flowering scrub.
    • : A colonial hill town and the usual base for the ProAves reserve nearby, which needs advance permission and a guide. The town itself is walked freely and its gardens hold canyon edge species.
    • : A sandstone colonial town on the canyon's southern rim, with streets and surrounding tracks walked freely. Swifts and swallows hawk over the plaza at dusk, and dry country species hold the scrub beyond town.
    • : The roadside town on the Medellin to Bogota highway nearest the Rio Claro reserve entrance, freely walked before booking the reserve itself. It is a convenient stop to check roadside wires and scrub for flycatchers.
    • : The regional city and usual base for trips into the Chicamocha canyon and out to Zapatoca, its parks and gardens free to walk. It is a practical stop for common garden species before heading into the canyon.
    • : A whitewashed colonial town on the Rio de Oro just outside Bucaramanga, with streets and riverside walked freely. Herons and kingfishers work the river through town.
  • Visitor centres: Fundacion ProAves
  • Also covers: Barichara, Bucaramanga, Chicamocha Canyon (Parque Nacional del Chicamocha), Doradal, Fundacion ProAves, Giron, Landazuri, Mesa de los Santos, ProAves Cucarachero de Chicamocha Reserve, Puerto Triunfo, Reserva Natural Canon del Rio Claro El Refugio, San Gil, Zapatoca
  • Also watch for: The Rio Claro karst holds caimans in its pools and guacharo colonies deep in its limestone caves, along with clouds of morpho and other large butterflies that are thickest in the drier months from December to March. The dry scrub of the Chicamocha canyon suits basking iguanas and, with patience, brocket deer at first light.

The Eastern Andes and Bogota

Paramo, cloud forest and wetland within two hours of the capital

The eastern range carries the capital at 2,600 metres, with paramo above it and cloud forest on both flanks. The city's own wetlands hold an endemic rail, and Chingaza's frailejon slopes are within a morning of the airport.

  • Habitat: Remnant temperate forest and shrub on the slopes above the savanna of Bogota, with wetland on the plateau floor at the city's edge.
  • When: Good all year. Bogota Rail, Apolinar's Wren and Green-bearded Helmetcrest hold the ground through the year.
  • Getting there: Parque La Florida lies at the end of the El Dorado airport runway: head out towards the airport and take the last turn on the right. For the temperate forest, take the road to Choachi about 50 km south-east, where a trail leaves the road before the top opposite the first house on the left, or ride the cable car to Monserrate and walk down to the same road.
  • Look for: Bogota Rail, Apolinar's Wren, Green-bearded Helmetcrest, Flame-winged Parakeet, Bronze-tailed Thornbill, Sword-billed Hummingbird
  • National parks: Chingaza National Natural Park, Sumapaz National Natural Park, Parque La Florida
  • Stops:
    • Observatorio de Colibries : A private hummingbird garden near La Calera, on paved road and a short unpaved stretch, visited by booking ahead. Feeders draw sword-billed hummingbird and a dozen other high Andean species at close range.
    • : A cloud forest lake on a signed track from the town of Tena. Day visits and short trails around the shore need no guide, and tanagers and flowerpiercers work the forest edge above the water.
    • Lagunas de Siecha : A paramo trail inside Chingaza's Guasca sector, open at weekends with a daily visitor cap and booked ahead through the park. Glacial lakes sit framed by frailejon, with Andean condor possible overhead.
    • : The reservoir at the heart of Chingaza's water supply system. The park road gives the view on a permit rather than free approach, and paramo ducks and the odd Andean condor pass over the open water.
    • : A colonial town on the road up to Chingaza's northern sector, freely walked and a natural stop for coffee before the climb. Rufous-collared sparrow and mountain birds work the gardens and hedgerows.
    • : The southern gateway town to Chingaza, free to reach by road before the park checkpoint. It is a good stop to scan the river valley for flycatchers and torrent duck.
    • Choachi and the Bogota eastern slope : The road east off the Bogota plateau. It drops through subparamo and cloud forest within an hour of the city.
  • Also covers: Chingaza National Natural Park, Choachi and the Bogota eastern slope, Embalse de Chuza, Fomeque, Guasca, La Calera, Laguna de Pedro Palo, Lagunas de Siecha, Observatorio de Colibries, Parque La Florida, Sumapaz National Natural Park, Tena
  • Also watch for: Chingaza and Sumapaz still hold spectacled bear, mountain tapir, puma and white-tailed deer, all shy and most likely at dawn on the quieter trails; sightings pick up in the drier spells of December to February and June to August when the paramo paths are firmer underfoot. Andean woolly monkeys and nocturnal monkeys turn up in the park's forested lower slopes.

The Central Andes: Manizales and Rio Blanco

Cloud forest and high paramo on the slopes of Nevado del Ruiz

The central range rises to the snow of Nevado del Ruiz, and the watershed reserve above the coffee city of Manizales has antpitta feeding stations in its forest. A paved road climbs from there to paramo at 4,000 metres, which makes this the easiest high altitude birding in the country.

  • Habitat: The Rio Blanco reserve covers nearly 5,000 hectares of mainly cloud forest and protects the water catchment for Manizales, and more than 350 bird species have been noted in it. Los Nevados National Park above the city runs from 2,600 to 5,300 metres through montane forest, high-altitude grassland, sub-paramo, paramo and glacier, with snow-capped peaks, an active volcano and over 200 high-altitude species.
  • When: Good all year. Brown-banded Antpitta, Bicolored Antpitta and Rusty-faced Parrot hold the ground through the year.
  • Getting there: Rio Blanco can be entered only by prior reservation through the Aguas de Manizales website, and visitors go accompanied by local guides. Los Nevados has accommodation within the park and in the vicinity, and high-altitude precautions matter there. Los Alcazares Ecopark on the edge of Manizales has four comfortable trails and an observation tower for canopy birding.
  • Look for: Brown-banded Antpitta, Bicolored Antpitta, Rusty-faced Parrot, Golden-plumed Parakeet, Andean Condor, Buff-winged Starfrontlet
  • National parks:
    • Los Nevados National Natural Park
    • Rio Blanco Ecological Reserve
    • Recinto del Pensamiento, A fee paying nature park on the road out of Manizales, with marked trails through orchid filled cloud forest that need no guide. A dedicated bird watching mirador looks over the canopy.
  • Stops:
    • : A private reserve run for Manizales' water utility, entered only with a booked guide who leads to the antpitta feeding points. Brown-banded antpitta and bicolored antpitta are the draw, called in at fixed stations.
    • : The regional city and usual base for Rio Blanco and the Nevado del Ruiz road, its cathedral hill and parks free to walk. It is a convenient stop before heading up into the reserve or the paramo.
    • : The last town on the road climbing from Manizales toward Los Nevados, with streets and outskirts walked freely. It is a natural staging point before the paramo, and tanagers and flowerpiercers hold the gardens.
    • Nevado del Ruiz : The snow capped volcano at the heart of Los Nevados park. The park road reaches its upper slopes on an entry fee and, in places, a guide, and high paramo specialists work the frailejon right up to the snowline.
  • Visitor centres:
    • Termales del Ruiz, A hotel and thermal spring at 3,500 metres inside Los Nevados park land, open to day visitors and overnight guests with no special permit. Paramo hummingbirds work the grounds and gardens.
  • Also covers: Los Nevados National Natural Park, Manizales, Murillo, Nevado del Ruiz, Recinto del Pensamiento, Rio Blanco Ecological Reserve, Rio Blanco Reserve trails, Termales del Ruiz, Villamaria
  • Also watch for: Spectacled bear and mountain tapir both range through the cloud forest of Rio Blanco and the lower slopes of Los Nevados. Fresh sign confirms them more often than a sighting does, and the drier months of December to February give the best trail conditions. Northern pudu and cougar are present and rarely seen. Andean condors reintroduced to the paramo are now a realistic sighting over the high ground, if an unpredictable one.

The Coffee Region: Otun Quimbaya and Montezuma

Sub-Andean and cloud forest on the flank of the Central and Western Andes, reached from Pereira by paved road and then a dirt military track

Coffee farms, bamboo and cloud forest on the Central and Western slopes, with a sanctuary river on one side and the long Montezuma road climbing Tatama on the other. Paved roads reach almost all of it.

  • Habitat: Otun Quimbaya sanctuary lies against the southwestern edge of Los Nevados National Park and is mostly wet secondary growth with montane and cloud forest between 1,800 and 2,200 metres, where 330 bird species have been observed. Tatama National Park, which the Montezuma road climbs into, covers over 520 square kilometres of largely undisturbed country from tropical rainforest to paramo between 2,000 and 4,200 metres and carries a list of more than 600 species.
  • When: Good all year. Cauca Guan, Gold-ringed Tanager and Chestnut Wood Quail hold the ground through the year.
  • Getting there: Otun Quimbaya is easy to reach from Pereira, and its community-run visitor centre has comfortable accommodation and well-trained guides. Access to Tatama is limited, so a visit is best organised through the national park office. Montezuma Rainforest at Pueblo Rico is the lodge that serves the ridge.
  • Look for: Cauca Guan, Gold-ringed Tanager, Chestnut Wood Quail, Tatama Tapaculo, Chami Antpitta
  • National parks:
    • Santuario de Fauna y Flora Otun Quimbaya, A national park run by Parques Nacionales, with an entry fee and reservation required. Guided walks leave the visitor centre at set times through the day.
    • Parque Natural Regional Ucumari, A regional park adjoining the sanctuary, with an entry fee payable at the gate. A rougher trail climbs through cloud forest toward the paramo.
    • Parque Nacional Natural Tatama
  • Stops:
    • : The hamlet at the sanctuary entrance, on a track along the Otun river. Hummingbird feeders and a footbridge mark the start of the trail.
    • : The coffee-region capital and the usual base for both Otun Quimbaya and the Montezuma road. Each is an hour or two away by car.
    • : A small Risaralda town on the way up from Pereira. It is the last proper stop for fuel and food before the road climbs toward Montezuma.
    • : The last town before the Montezuma road climbs into Tatama. It has basic lodging and is the usual place to arrange a guide for the park.
    • Montezuma road : A dirt military track through Tatama National Park, walked from the entrance gate near the army post. An entry fee and reservation are required and a guide is strongly recommended. Birding runs dawn until mid afternoon.
    • Cerro Montezuma, Tatama National Park : The high point of the road inside the national park. Elfin cloud forest here holds the region's rarest western-Andes endemics.
  • Visitor centres: CARDER, Corporacion Autonoma Regional de Risaralda
  • Also covers: CARDER, Corporacion Autonoma Regional de Risaralda, Cerro Montezuma, Tatama National Park, La Suiza, Montezuma road, Parque Nacional Natural Tatama, Parque Natural Regional Ucumari, Pereira, Pueblo Rico, Salento, Santuario de Fauna y Flora Otun Quimbaya
  • Also watch for: Colombian red howler monkeys are the sanctuary's other flagship animal at Otun Quimbaya. They roar from the canopy most mornings and are easiest to hear at dawn. Camera traps in Tatama National Park turn up more Andean bears than anywhere else on this slope, along with the Colombian weasel, a creature so rare that only a handful of specimens have ever been studied, all from this same stretch of forest.

The Western Andes and Jardin

Cloud forest and wax-palm cattle country on the western slope of the Andes around a colonial coffee town, reached by paved road from Medellin

A whitewashed town with a cock-of-the-rock lek a few minutes' walk from the square, and wax palm valleys above it where the Yellow-eared Parrot came back from the edge. Antioquia's best birding is here.

  • Habitat: Las Tangaras Reserve at El Carmen de Atrato covers 2,900 hectares of tropical forest ecosystems from 1,250 to 3,000 metres on the northern edge of the West Andes, at the natural border between the Colombian interior and the Choco, and more than 250 species have been observed there. The Colibri del Sol reserve holds nearly 730 hectares of northern West Andean montane forest and paramo between 2,700 and 3,800 metres, a wet and cloudy place with at least 370 species.
  • When: Good all year. Yellow-eared Parrot, Gold-ringed Tanager and Munchique Wood Wren stay through the year.
  • Getting there: Las Tangaras lies some 140 km south of Medellin, with accommodation booked outside the reserve and guides available. Colibri del Sol has limited accommodation and guides at hand. Around Jardin the birding runs on private reserves, among them the Gallito de Roca reserve, the Loro Orejiamarillo reserve and Mirador el Roble.
  • Look for: Yellow-eared Parrot, Gold-ringed Tanager, Munchique Wood Wren, Black-and-gold Tanager, Velvet-purple Coronet
  • National parks: Reserva Natural de las Aves Loro Orejiamarillo, Reserva Natural de la Sociedad Civil Mesenia-Paramillo, Reserva Natural de las Aves Las Tangaras
  • Stops:
    • : A colonial coffee town in southwest Antioquia and the usual base for the region. Tanagers and euphonias move through the trees around the plaza.
    • Reserva Loro Orejiamarillo : A ProAves reserve booked in advance, with simple cabin lodging. Yellow-eared Parrots gather to roost and feed in the wax palm cloud forest.
    • : A private civil-society reserve near Jardin, visited by arrangement with the owners. Gold-ringed Tanager and mixed flocks move through wet forest.
    • Las Tangaras : A ProAves reserve on the Choco side of the range, most of a day's drive from Jardin and booked ahead for lodging. Black-and-gold Tanager comes to hummingbird feeders on the porch.
    • : The Choco village and gateway below Las Tangaras, by 4x4 from Medellin. It is the last stop for supplies before the reserve track.
    • : A town on the far side of the wax palm corridor from Jardin. It marks the southern edge of Yellow-eared Parrot country.
    • Urrao and the Colibri del Sol reserve : Paramo and elfin forest above Urrao, protected for the Dusky Starfrontlet. The bird was described from here and lives on this massif alone.
  • Visitor centres: Fundacion ProAves de Colombia
  • Also covers: Andes, El Carmen de Atrato, Fundacion ProAves de Colombia, Jardin, Medellin, Reserva Loro Orejiamarillo, Reserva Mesenia-Paramillo, Reserva Natural de la Sociedad Civil Mesenia-Paramillo, Reserva Natural de las Aves Las Tangaras, Reserva Natural de las Aves Loro Orejiamarillo, Riosucio, Caldas, Urrao and the Colibri del Sol reserve
  • Also watch for: Andean bears cross the cloud forest at the Loro Orejiamarillo reserve and turn up more often on camera traps than in person. Wax palms around Jardin hold fruit for much of the year, and Yellow-eared Parrots gather in loose flocks to feed on them, most reliably watched in the early morning before the cloud closes in.

The Cauca valley and the Km 18 cloud forest

Cloud forest on a paved road forty minutes above Cali, dropping through Pacific-slope foothill forest to a wetland on the dry Cauca valley floor

A sugar valley with cloud forest on the road above Cali and Pacific foothill forest dropping away west of it. Family fincas along the ridge keep feeders that bring whole mixed flocks into view.

  • Habitat: A shallow lake and its marsh on the floor of the Cauca valley, with wet cloud forest on the western cordillera above Cali where the road climbs towards the Pacific.
  • When: Good all year. Multicolored Tanager, Andean Cock-of-the-rock and Toucan Barbet are on site in all twelve months.
  • Getting there: Buga is 45 km north of Cali; head west towards the Rio Cauca bridge and Buenaventura, and the road runs 4 km along the north shore of the Laguna de Sonso with open views. The cloud forest is on the Cali to Buenaventura road above the city.
  • Look for: Multicolored Tanager, Andean Cock-of-the-rock, Toucan Barbet, Long-wattled Umbrellabird, Horned Screamer
  • National parks:
    • Parque Nacional Natural Farallones de Cali, A national park whose boundary runs along the Km 18 ridge. An entry fee and reservation are required beyond the roadside strip, and Cock-of-the-rock and Toucan Barbet hold the mist forest.
    • Laguna de Sonso, A wetland reserve on the Cauca River floodplain, on a raised path from the entrance. Horned Screamer and waterbirds hold the open water and gallery forest.
    • San Cipriano forest reserve
    • Parque Nacional Natural Purace, Paramo and elfin forest on a live volcano east of Popayan. A condor viewing point sits above the visitor area.
  • Stops:
    • : A farmed hillside and forest patch along the Km 18 road above Cali, birded from the verge and short paths. No permit is needed to walk the road.
    • : A family finca at Km 18 charging a small fee for its hummingbird feeders. Turn up and pay at the gate for coffee among a dozen hummingbird species.
    • : A lower, hotter road down the Pacific slope past the Bajo Anchicaya dam, birded slowly from a vehicle or on foot. Permission is needed to pass the dam gate.
    • : A rainforest village reached only by brujita rail carts on an old logging line. A community-run reserve surrounds it, with river tubing and lowland Choco birds.
    • Pichinde valley : A valley road west of Cali climbing towards Farallones. It is quieter than Km 18 and holds the same slope.
  • Visitor centres: DAGMA, Departamento Administrativo de Gestion del Medio Ambiente (Cali)
  • Also covers: Anchicaya road, Buenaventura, Buga, DAGMA, Departamento Administrativo de Gestion del Medio Ambiente (Cali), Dagua, Finca Alejandria, Laguna de Sonso, Parque Nacional Natural Farallones de Cali, Parque Nacional Natural Purace, Pichinde valley, Popayan, San Antonio, San Cipriano forest reserve
  • Also watch for: Farallones de Cali holds white-tailed deer, spectacled bears and mountain tapirs on its higher ridges, though these stay well back from the roadside trails and are rarely seen by passing birders. San Cipriano's rainforest is a stronghold for blue morpho butterflies and glass frogs, most active in the wetter months of April, May, October and November.

Narino and the southern Pacific slope

Pacific slope forest above Tumaco and the descent into Putumayo, on the road to Ecuador

The Pacific slope in Narino carries a set of birds that reaches its northern limit here and its southern limit in Ecuador. Rio Nambi and La Planada sit on the same slope at different heights, and the road east from Pasto drops through the eastern Andes into Amazonian Putumayo in a single morning.

  • Habitat: Wet Choco forest on the Pacific slope, from the 3,600 ha reserve at La Planada at 1,800 m down through the Rio Nambi and Rio Ramos valleys, with a 25 km stretch of forest between 1,800 and 2,300 m on the Pasto to Mocoa road.
  • Getting there: La Planada is reached from Ricaurte on the Pasto to Tumaco road. Ask at Rio Nambi for a guide and take supplies for camping. The Narino to Putumayo border stretch is one-way and demands the most experienced driver, or the bus.
  • Look for: Chestnut-crowned Antpitta, Andean Cock-of-the-rock, Crested Quetzal, Masked Saltator, Gold-ringed Tanager
  • National park:
    • Reserva Natural La Planada, Cloud forest at 1,800 metres on the Pacific slope above Ricaurte. It is run as a reserve with trails and simple lodging.
  • Stops:
    • Reserva Natural Rio Nambi : Lower Pacific slope forest below La Planada, on the Tumaco road. It holds the foothill birds the higher reserve misses.
    • The Pasto to Mocoa road : The descent from the eastern Andes into Amazonian Putumayo. Pullouts along its length give the birding.
  • Also covers: Barbacoas, Reserva Natural La Planada, Reserva Natural Rio Nambi, Ricaurte, The Pasto to Mocoa road, Tumaco
  • Also watch for: Spectacled bear in the Narino cloud forest, and the Pacific slope amphibian list that makes these reserves a herpetological destination too.

The Choco and the Pacific coast

Rainforest meeting the Pacific, reached only by small plane or boat from Medellin

Rainforest meets the ocean on a coast with no road to it. A small plane or a boat is how you arrive. It is among the wettest places on earth and one of the richest, with humpbacks calving offshore for half the year.

  • Habitat: Utria National Park spreads over 544 square kilometres along the Pacific shore of the Choco and protects the coastal strip and the ocean beside it. The land is covered by a thick carpet of tropical rainforest, the park is renowned for its orchids, and more than 440 bird species are listed. Whales and turtles are easy to see in season.
  • Getting there: Getting to the national park is challenging and worth the effort. It is best reached by boat from Bahia Solano or El Valle. Accommodation is available at the visitor centre inside the park and guides are at hand.
  • Look for: Baudo Guan, Sapayoa, Berlepsch's Tinamou, Choco Toucan, Choco Trogon, Great Curassow
  • National park: Parque Nacional Natural Utria
  • Stops:
    • : The small airstrip that is the main gateway to the northern Choco coast, on short flights from Medellin. Forest edge and coastal birding start right at the runway.
    • : A small Pacific coast town, by air from Medellin or by boat from Buenaventura. It is the usual launch point for boat trips into the Golfo de Tribuga and Utria.
    • : A fishing village on the open Pacific coast, by road from Bahia Solano. Beach and forest trails are walked independently from the village itself.
    • : A beach south of El Valle backed by private forest lodges that keep their own trails, open to walkers for a fee. Humpback whales show offshore from July to November.
    • Ensenada de Utria boat channel : A national park entered by boat through a narrow mangrove-lined channel, with an entry fee and a ranger station. Whales calve inside the ensenada from August to October.
    • : A coastal village south of Nuqui, on foot or by boat. Its forest trail and hot spring are walked with a local guide, through primary rainforest with mixed understorey flocks.
    • : The northernmost point of the Choco coast, on a long boat trip from Bahia Solano. It is used as a whale watching viewpoint at the peak of the season.
  • Also covers: Bahia Solano airport, Cabo Marzo, El Valle, Ensenada de Utria boat channel, Nuqui, Parque Nacional Natural Utria, Playa El Almejal, Termales
  • Also watch for: Humpback whales arrive to calve and nurse from July to November, with the peak of sightings in the Golfo de Tribuga and Ensenada de Utria running August to October. Spider monkeys and howler monkeys move through the forest canopy, and olive ridley sea turtles nest on the open Pacific beaches from around September into December.

The Llanos: Meta and Casanare

Seasonally flooded savanna and gallery forest on working cattle ranches, reached by road from Yopal or Villavicencio

Flooded savanna running east towards the Orinoco, worked as cattle country and birded from the same ranches. Waterbirds gather in numbers that few other places in South America can show.

  • Habitat: The Llanos are vast eastern savannas running from the East Andes to the Venezuelan border, and the northern parts flood seasonally into wide shallow water. Bosque Bavaria northwest of Villavicencio holds 30 hectares of well-preserved humid tropical foothill forest between 470 and 650 metres, with adjoining protected land climbing to 1,100 metres and nearly 400 species recorded. Serrania de la Macarena National Park covers 6,293 square kilometres of rainforest, tropical dry forest and shrub savanna where the Amazon, the Llanos and the East Andes meet, and its list runs past 500 species.
  • When: Good all year. Jabiru, Sharp-tailed Ibis and Horned Screamer are here in every month.
  • Getting there: Distances out here are long and reaching the sites takes time, so flying from Bogota is the sensible way in, except for the places along the eastern foothills of the East Andes. Villavicencio is the capital of the Llanos and puts several good sites within easy reach, with accommodation of all classes in the city. The buffer zones around Macarena are best entered through Macarena town by air, and the Casanare reserves including Hato La Aurora are reached via Yopal.
  • Look for: Orinoco Goose, Jabiru, Sharp-tailed Ibis, Horned Screamer, Orinoco Softtail, Scarlet Macaw
  • National parks:
    • Parque Nacional Natural Sierra de la Macarena, A national park entered only with a certified local guide from La Macarena town, which is a permit requirement. Andean, Amazon and Orinoco habitats meet on one sandstone range.
    • Parque Nacional Natural Serrania de Manacacias
  • Stops:
    • : A working cattle hato in the flooded Casanare savanna that takes overnight guests by advance booking, with its own guides and horses. Orinoco goose, jabiru and sharp-tailed ibis hold the lagoons.
    • : The nearest town to Hato La Aurora, by road from Yopal. It is the fuel and supply stop before the final stretch of dirt track to the hato.
    • : The Casanare departmental capital, with the regional airport. It is the gateway town for the eastern llanos, and savanna and gallery forest birding starts on the roads leaving the city.
    • : The Meta departmental capital, where the Andean foothills drop into the plains, by road or air from Bogota. It is the base before heading further into the llanos.
    • : The river town serving as the only gateway to the national park, on a small plane from Villavicencio or Bogota. Boats are hired locally for the Cano Cristales river.
    • : A river port on the Rio Meta, by road from Villavicencio. Boats can be hired for the day to watch Orinoco river dolphins and giant otters along the banks.
  • Also covers: La Macarena town, Parque Nacional Natural Serrania de Manacacias, Parque Nacional Natural Sierra de la Macarena, Paz de Ariporo, Puerto Gaitan, Reserva Natural Hato La Aurora, Villavicencio, Yopal
  • Also watch for: Orinoco crocodiles, once close to disappearing from Casanare, survive on a few of the working hatos that now run head-start and release programs for them, alongside capybara herds, giant anteaters and anacondas. The dry season from December to March draws animals to the shrinking waterholes and gives the easiest viewing, while the plains flood again with the rains from April.

The Amazon: Leticia and Amacayacu

Flooded Amazon rainforest and river islands, reached only by boat or a flight to Leticia

The southern tip of the country, where Colombia, Peru and Brazil meet on the river. Birding here is by boat, on river islands and in terra firme, the forest above the flood line, and the indigenous communities guide it themselves.

  • Habitat: Amacayacu National Park is Colombia's most southerly park and borders the Amazon river and Peru. It extends over 2,935 square kilometres of tropical rainforest and floodplain forest between 100 and 330 metres, and about 500 bird species have been recorded in it.
  • When: Good all year. Hoatzin, Pied Plover and White-eared Jacamar are here in every month.
  • Getting there: The indigenous village of Puerto Narino is the best entry point to the region and is reached from Leticia by a two-hour boat ride on the Amazon river. The village runs community-based ecotourism and offers accommodation and guides.
  • Look for: Hoatzin, Zigzag Heron, Agami Heron, Point-tailed Palmcreeper, Pied Plover, White-eared Jacamar
  • National parks: Parque Nacional Natural Amacayacu, Complejo de Humedales Lagos de Tarapoto (Ramsar site)
  • Stops:
    • : The Amazonas departmental capital and the only entry point by commercial flight. It is a river port town and the base before heading upriver or to the reserves.
    • : A car-free river town, a two to three hour boat trip from Leticia. It is the base for visiting Amacayacu, Lagos de Tarapoto and nearby indigenous communities.
    • Amacayacu visitor dock : A national park entered by boat from Leticia, with an entry fee and ranger-led trails. Boardwalks run through flooded forest to a canopy tower over the Amazon river.
    • : A Ramsar-listed lake and wetland complex, by boat from Puerto Narino. Paddling it quietly at dawn brings pink river dolphins and the skulking marsh and swamp forest birds.
    • : A Ticuna indigenous community inside the buffer zone of Amacayacu. A community guide and permit are required to walk the village trails and canopy tower.
    • : An Amazon river island reached by boat. It is birded from the water along its flooded forest edge as the boat passes between Leticia and Puerto Narino.
    • Parque Natural Tanimboca : A private forest reserve at Kilometro 11 outside Leticia, entered for a fee, with its own canopy walkway and trails. It is useful for terra firme forest birding near town.
  • Visitor centres: Mundo Amazonico, Fundacion Omacha
  • Also covers: Amacayacu visitor dock, Complejo de Humedales Lagos de Tarapoto (Ramsar site), Fundacion Omacha, Isla de los Micos, Leticia, Mocagua, Mundo Amazonico, Parque Nacional Natural Amacayacu, Parque Natural Tanimboca, Puerto Narino
  • Also watch for: Pink and gray river dolphins work the main river and its oxbow lakes year round, most easily watched from Puerto Narino or on the water at Lagos de Tarapoto. The Amazon's water level swings between a high-water, flooded-forest season around May to July and a low-water season around September to November that exposes river beaches and sandbars used by turtles and caimans.

Frequently Asked Questions

When is the best time to go birding in Colombia?

December to March is the driest across the north and the Andes and the most reliable overall, and it also holds the northern migrants. July and August bring a shorter dry spell to the coffee region. Birds are present all year; the season decides the roads and the afternoons rather than the list.

Do I need a guide?

For most of Colombia, yes, and it is worth it. Several of the best reserves are private and take visitors by arrangement, the endemics are local and often silent by mid morning, and a Colombian guide knows which roads are open. Bogota, the coffee region towns and the Santa Marta foothills can all be birded independently.

How many species does Colombia have?

More than any other country. The card wall here carries every species BeakBrain records in Colombia, and the figure in the header is counted from that list rather than typed.

Are there places to stay listed above?

No. No Colombian property is priced or certified against a public register, and a list of city hotels would say nothing useful about where to sleep near birds. The region cards carry the sites and the parks instead.

Is it safe?

The birding regions above are visited routinely and most have a local guiding economy built around them. Conditions vary by department and change, so read your own government's current travel advice for the specific areas you plan to visit, and take local advice on roads in the Perija, the Choco interior and parts of the Llanos.

How much altitude will I be at?

Bogota sits at 2,600 metres and the paramo sites above Manizales reach 4,000. Altitude sickness is a real consideration on a trip that flies in and drives straight up, so build a night at middle elevation into the start rather than going high on day one.

What about the rain?

Andean rain usually arrives in the afternoon, which suits birding: the best hours are the first three after dawn anyway. The Choco is different, with several metres of rain a year and no dry month, so pack for it rather than plan around it.

How do the internal flights work?

Colombia is long and mountainous and the domestic network is good, so most itineraries fly between blocks rather than drive. Santa Marta, Bogota, Pereira, Manizales, Medellin, Cali and Leticia all have airports, and the Choco strips at Nuqui and Bahia Solano take small aircraft that depend on weather.

Which region should a first visit choose?

The coffee region between Pereira, Manizales and Jardin. It is paved throughout, holds cloud forest, paramo, a cock-of-the-rock lek and the wax palm valleys within a few hours of each other, and it needs no permits.

Can I bird here with limited mobility?

Often yes, and it varies by site. A good deal of the birding here happens from roadsides, hides and lodge grounds rather than on long walks, and some reserves keep flat, surfaced trails. Ask a lodge or reserve directly about step free access, surfaces and seating before you book. The Birdability Map records those details for birding sites, and their Access Considerations guide lists the questions worth asking. Coverage is thin outside the United States, so read a blank area as unrecorded rather than unsuitable.

Birding Community

Alongside the national bodies below, Colombia has 10 local bird clubs across 8 regions. See every Colombian club by region.
